passage: Note from the Class 4 teacher. Pema came to the staffroom at short break with a hundred-rupee note clenched in her fist and pink cheeks. She had found it near the water taps. She told me that for a whole minute she had thought about the sparkly erasers at the stationery stall and an ice lolly, and her friend Varun, walking beside her, had said she could just keep it. "But somebody must be looking for it," she said. She looked sorry to let it go, and then a bit lighter. I thanked her and we wrote a notice asking whoever had lost money to come and tell me how much it was.

qa.q: Where did Pema find the hundred-rupee note?
qa.a: She found it near the water taps.

qa.q: What was Pema feeling as she carried the note in her fist to the staffroom?
qa.a: She was pulled two ways: she wanted what the money could buy, but she also thought somebody must be looking for it; she looked sorry to let it go and then lighter.

qa.q: How could the teacher make sure the money reaches its real owner?
qa.a: Put up a notice asking whoever lost money to come and say how much it was, so the owner can be told apart from anyone else.

qa.q: How might the child who lost the note be feeling at this moment?
qa.a: Probably worried or upset, checking pockets and bags, so the notice gives them hope of getting it back.

grounding: Illustrates a child tempted by found money who hands it to a teacher.

passage: On the dusty road to Kotla school, Ritu spotted a folded fifty-rupee note beside a drain. She picked it up, and her mind went to whoever had dropped it. Maybe a child sent to buy something for their mother, walking along, patting pockets, getting more frightened at every step. At the school gate she saw Zubin, red-eyed, turning out his bag for the peon. His mother had given him money for a notebook, he was saying. Ritu held out the note. "Is this yours?" Zubin stared, then his whole face cleared. "Yes! Thank you!" Ritu walked into class feeling warm, as if she had been handed something, not lost it.

qa.q: What had Zubin's mother given him money for?
qa.a: She had given him money for a notebook.

qa.q: What was Ritu imagining that made giving the note back feel simple?
qa.a: She pictured whoever dropped it walking along, patting their pockets and getting more frightened at every step, so returning it felt warm rather than like a loss.

qa.q: What would you advise Ritu to do if she found money and could not see who lost it?
qa.a: Hand it to a teacher or the school peon and say where she found it, so they can ask around.

qa.q: How did Zubin see the moment Ritu held out the note?
qa.a: As a huge relief: he was red-eyed and turning out his bag, so his whole face cleared when the note came back.

grounding: Illustrates a child imagining the worry of whoever lost money, which makes returning it feel warm.

passage: Outside the tea shop in the kasba, Jeevan picked up a crumpled twenty-rupee note. "Finders keepers!" said Rashmi, and two other kids joined in. "Chips! Chips!" Jeevan's fingers closed around the note. He wanted them to like him, and he also knew it was somebody's. "Let's ask the tea shop uncle if anyone lost it," he said, his voice a little shaky. A groan went up and someone rolled their eyes, but Rashmi shrugged. "Fine, ask." Later, when the others had run ahead, Rashmi said quietly, "I didn't feel right about it either."

qa.q: What kind of note did Jeevan pick up?
qa.a: He picked up a crumpled twenty-rupee note.

qa.q: Why was Jeevan's voice shaky when he suggested asking the tea shop uncle?
qa.a: He was torn between wanting the group to like him and knowing the note belonged to somebody, and he may have feared their reaction.

qa.q: What small step let Jeevan say no without a fight?
qa.a: He offered a simple alternative, asking the tea shop uncle whether anyone had lost it, instead of lecturing his friends.

qa.q: How might Rashmi have seen that moment?
qa.a: Rashmi joined the cheer at first, but later admitted not feeling right about it either, so was probably quietly relieved that someone said it.

grounding: Illustrates a child torn between friends' finders-keepers pressure and doing right, declining politely.

passage: Arohi handed Kamal a hundred-rupee note for a packet of biscuits for her grandmother. The shop was noisy with customers, and Kamal was already calling out to the next one. She counted the change as she walked away. It was ten rupees too much. Nobody will know, she thought, and then, but I will. Her cheeks went hot. She turned back through the crowd. "Kamal uncle, you gave me too much." He counted, laughed, and shook his head at himself. "So I did! Thank you, beta." Arohi's face was still warm from embarrassment, but her steps felt light. Next time Kamal let her drop the biscuits into the bag herself.

qa.q: How much extra change did Arohi receive?
qa.a: It was ten rupees too much.

qa.q: How did Arohi feel as she walked away with the extra change?
qa.a: Arohi felt guilty: she thought nobody would know, then that she would, and her cheeks went hot, so she turned back.

qa.q: What would you advise a child who notices extra change and feels awkward about giving it back?
qa.a: Say it plainly and politely, expecting a moment of awkwardness that passes quickly.

qa.q: How might Kamal have seen the moment when Arohi came back?
qa.a: It was an honest mistake in a busy shop, so he laughed at himself and thanked her, and letting her pack the bag next time showed he trusted her 🙂.

grounding: Illustrates a child returning extra change from a shopkeeper and feeling awkward, then light and trusted.

passage: Parent-teacher day at school. The class teacher said to Manjula's mother, "Your daughter took a lost wallet to the office last week, from the canteen table." Mummy pulled Manjula into a hug right there in the corridor. Manjula's face went hot and she grinned. Later, on the bench outside, she told her friend Shreya, "I wasn't thinking about a hug when I took it in. It just wasn't mine." Shreya asked, "Would you have taken it in if nobody ever knew?" Manjula thought. "Yes. But the hug was nice too." She looked pleased and a bit shy about it.

qa.q: Where had Manjula found the wallet?
qa.a: It was on a canteen table.

qa.q: What was Manjula feeling after her mother's hug?
qa.a: Proud and happy, but clear that she had taken the wallet in because it was not hers, not for praise; she looked pleased and a bit shy.

qa.q: What could Manjula do if she does the right thing again and nobody praises her?
qa.a: Keep doing it anyway, remembering that she did it because it was not hers, and that the good feeling comes from inside her too 😊.

qa.q: How does Manjula's mother see the news?
qa.a: She is proud and wants to show it straight away, hugging Manjula in the corridor; it shows she cares about the kind of person Manjula is.

grounding: Illustrates a child proud of a parent's hug for returning a wallet, while knowing honesty matters even without praise.

passage:
"Is this yours?" Bhupen held out a folded note.
"My lunch money!" Alka had been checking every pocket for ten minutes. "Where was it?"
"Under the bench."
"Thank you, thank you! Take half my sandwich, please."
"No, it's fine. Eat it."
At home Bhupen told Mama, "Alka thanked me three times."
"How did that feel?"
"Really good. But I wish I didn't keep hoping for it. I think I'd have given it back anyway."
"Would you?"
"Yes. I think it would still feel right, only quieter."

qa.q: Where was Alka's lunch money?
qa.a: It was under the bench.

qa.q: What does Bhupen feel when Alka thanks him, and what does he tell himself about it?
qa.a: He feels really good, but he tells himself not to keep hoping for thanks each time; he thinks giving it back would still feel right, only quieter.

qa.q: What could Bhupen do if nobody thanks him next time?
qa.a: He can remember that returning the money was right on its own, and let the quiet good feeling be enough.

qa.q: How might Alka have been feeling before Bhupen held out the note?
qa.a: Worried about the lost lunch money, since Alka had been checking every pocket for ten minutes, so the thanks came out of relief.

grounding: Illustrates a child thanked for returning money who learns not to expect a reward every time.

passage: Sunday morning in the Chandigarh gurdwara, the keertan began and the whole hall sang together. Sarika sat cross-legged between Bebe and her cousin Irawati, her head covered with a soft orange scarf. She did not know every word yet, but she hummed along, and her chest felt full, as if all those voices were carrying her. Afterwards, at the shoe rack, she tugged Bebe's sleeve. "Bebe, why do we cover our heads?" Bebe smiled and slowed down. "Let's ask Giani ji together," she said, "and you can tell me what you think of his answer."

qa.q: Who did Sarika sit between at the gurdwara?
qa.a: She sat between Bebe and her cousin Irawati.

qa.q: What was Sarika feeling while the hall sang, and what was she also wondering?
qa.a: She felt happy and connected, her chest full as if all the voices were carrying her; she was also wondering why they cover their heads.

qa.q: How could Sarika get her question answered in a respectful way?
qa.a: Ask kindly after the service, with real curiosity, first from Bebe and then from Giani ji.

qa.q: How might Bebe see Sarika's question?
qa.a: Bebe smiled and slowed down, so she probably sees it as a good sign that Sarika is paying attention and wants to understand, not just copy.

grounding: Illustrates a child feeling belonging in communal singing and also asking why things are done.

passage: Dusk in the village, and the lamp was lit in the courtyard. Dadi sat on the charpai with Raghav beside her while his cousin Hemant dozed against the wall. She sang one short evening prayer, line by line, and Raghav repeated it, tripping over the long words. Her eyes shone in the lamplight. "Again," she said softly, and he did it again. That night he lay awake, wondering what one line meant. Next morning he asked her. Dadi laughed. "I'm glad you asked. I'll tell you what my mother told me, and then you can think about it yourself."

qa.q: Who dozed against the wall while Dadi taught the prayer?
qa.a: His cousin Hemant dozed against the wall.

qa.q: What was Raghav feeling as he repeated the prayer, and what is the evidence?
qa.a: He seemed to feel loved and settled: he kept repeating the line even when tripping over words, and he cared enough to wonder about its meaning afterwards.

qa.q: What could Raghav do with his questions about the prayer?
qa.a: Keep taking the prayer in respectfully and ask Dadi about it when he can, as he did next morning.

qa.q: How might Dadi feel when Raghav asks about a line?
qa.a: She seems glad, since she laughed and said she was glad he asked, so she probably sees questions as part of learning, not as disrespect.

grounding: Illustrates a child taught a prayer by his grandmother, feeling loved, and later asking a question that is welcomed.

passage: I'm Mehak, and I go to Sunday class at the community hall with my friend Disha. Our religious teacher tells stories, and Disha listens with her chin on her hands and does not blink. Last week the story was about a man who fed hungry animals in the rain. All the way home Disha told it to me again, sure that every part happened exactly as told. This week the story was about a punishment for children who miss prayers. Disha went very quiet. She said she would ask her mother about it. I could not tell if it was still bothering her by evening.

qa.q: Where do Mehak and Disha go on Sundays?
qa.a: They go to Sunday class at the community hall.

qa.q: What did Disha seem to feel about the stories, and what changed with the punishment story?
qa.a: She seemed to trust the stories completely, but the punishment story made her very quiet and probably worried, though Mehak could not be sure what she was thinking.

qa.q: What could Disha do about the story that unsettled her?
qa.a: Ask her mother, as she said she would, and notice how stories about kindness feel different from stories that only frighten.

qa.q: How might the religious teacher see Disha in class?
qa.a: As an attentive child who takes the stories in fully; the teacher may not know that one story worried her.

grounding: Illustrates a child fully trusting a religious teacher's stories, with a first small sign of noticing a frightening one.

passage: Monday. Before opening his tiffin, Tejas folded his hands and whispered thanks for his family and the aloo parathas, as he did every day. Warmth settled in his chest. Wednesday. Hrithik sat beside him with a tiffin holding just two dry rotis and turned away when Tejas glanced over. Tejas made his thank-you shorter that day and kept thinking about that tiffin all afternoon. Friday. Tejas whispered his thanks, then tore a paratha in half and slid it onto the lid of Hrithik's tiffin. "Mummy packs too many anyway," he said. Hrithik grinned, and Tejas felt the same warmth, only bigger.

qa.q: What was in Tejas's tiffin on Monday?
qa.a: It held aloo parathas.

qa.q: What was Tejas thinking about on Wednesday afternoon?
qa.a: He kept thinking about Hrithik's tiffin with just two dry rotis, which suggests he was uncomfortable about having so much when a friend had little.

qa.q: What small step did Tejas take on Friday, and why does it fit his thanks?
qa.a: He tore a paratha in half and shared it with Hrithik, turning his thankfulness into something he could do 🙂.

qa.q: How might Hrithik have felt about the shared paratha?
qa.a: Hrithik turned away on Wednesday, perhaps embarrassed, so the easy way Tejas shared, saying his Mummy packs too many, may have made it simple to accept; the grin suggests he was glad.

grounding: Illustrates a child thankful to God before eating who turns that gratitude into sharing food.
